claims.text: What the strip looks like ST-segment elevation in two or more contiguous leads over the damaged area; reciprocal depression may be present in other leads.
claims.quote: showing ST-segment elevation ≥ 1 mm in 2 or more contiguous leads subtending the damaged area; or in V2-V3 ≥ 2 mm in males 40 years or older, ≥ 2.5 mm in males younger than 40 years, and 1.5 mm in females of all ages (1). Reciprocal depression may be present in other leads.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) STEMI criteria: ST elevation at the J point in two contiguous leads — ≥ 1 mm in most leads; ≥ 2 mm (men) or ≥ 1.5 mm (women) in V2–V3
claims.quote: Criteria (new guidelines): ST elevation at the J point in two contiguous leads: ≥ 1 mm in most leads ≥ 2 mm (men) or ≥ 1.5 mm (women) in V2–V3

claims.text: Posterior and right-sided leads: ≥ 0.5 mm in V7–V9 (posterior) or V3R–V4R (right-sided)
claims.quote: ≥ 0.5 mm in V7–V9 (posterior) or V3R–V4R (right-sided)

claims.text: Q waves: pathologic Q waves often develop over time but are not needed for the diagnosis
claims.quote: Pathologic Q waves often develop over time but are not necessary for the diagnosis

claims.text: Pitfall: ST elevation may be subtle, especially in the inferior leads — attention can wrongly go to the leads with ST depression
claims.quote: The ECG must be read carefully because ST-segment elevation may be subtle, particularly in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF); sometimes the reader’s attention is mistakenly focused on leads with ST-segment depression.

claims.text: With symptoms, ST elevation has a specificity of 98 to 99% and a sensitivity of 35 to 56% for MI
claims.quote: If symptoms are present, ST-segment elevation on ECG has a specificity of 98 to 99% and a sensitivity of 35 to 56% for diagnosing myocardial infarction

claims.text: Timing: the ECG is the most important test — do it as soon as possible (e.g., within 10 minutes of arrival)
claims.quote: ECG is the most important test and should be performed as soon as possible (eg, within 10 minutes of presentation).

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) Mechanism: transmural infarcts involve the full wall thickness and usually give ST elevation and, later, abnormal Q waves
claims.quote: Transmural infarcts involve the whole thickness of myocardium from epicardium to endocardium and are usually characterized by ST-segment elevation and, later, by the development of abnormal Q waves on ECG.

claims.text: Type 1 MI: a primary coronary event (e.g., plaque rupture, erosion or fissuring; coronary dissection); type 2: increased oxygen demand (e.g., hypertension) or decreased supply (e.g., spasm, embolism, arrhythmia, hypotension)
claims.quote: Type 1: Spontaneous MI caused by ischemia due to a primary coronary event (eg, plaque rupture, erosion, or fissuring; coronary dissection) Type 2: Ischemia due to increased oxygen demand (eg, hypertension) or decreased supply (eg, coronary artery spasm or embolism, arrhythmia, hypotension)

claims.text: Symptoms Often the first symptom: deep substernal pressure or aching, often radiating to the back, jaw, arms or shoulders; like stable angina but usually more severe and longer, more often with dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea or vomiting, and relieved little or only briefly by rest or nitroglycerin
claims.quote: Often, the first symptom of infarction is deep, substernal, visceral pain, described as aching or pressure, often radiating to the back, jaw, left arm, right arm, shoulders, or all of these areas. The pain is similar to stable angina but is usually more severe and long-lasting; more often accompanied by dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, and/or vomiting; and relieved little or only temporarily by rest or nitroglycerin.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Acute MI

claims.text: In the general population about 20% of acute MIs are silent; up to 30% may be silent with diabetes
claims.quote: in the general population, approximately 20% of acute MIs are silent (2, 3), and up to 30% may be silent in patients with diabetes
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Acute MI

claims.text: Chest pain predominates in both sexes, but females more often have additional symptoms and atypical pain; older patients may report dyspnea more than ischemic chest pain
claims.quote: Chest pain is the predominant symptom in both males and females, but females are more likely to experience additional symptoms and atypical chest pain, and they are less likely to have prodromal symptoms attributed to heart disease (4). Older patients may report dyspnea more than ischemic-type chest pain (5).
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Acute MI

claims.text: Exam: skin may be pale, cool and diaphoretic; pulse may be thready; blood pressure varies, though many patients are initially somewhat hypertensive during pain
claims.quote: Skin may be pale, cool, and diaphoretic. Peripheral or central cyanosis may be present. Pulse may be thready, and blood pressure is variable, although many patients initially have some degree of hypertension during pain.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Acute MI

claims.text: A fourth heart sound (S4) is almost universally present
claims.quote: a fourth heart sound (S4) is almost universally present
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Acute MI

claims.text: Treatment Prehospital: IV access, oxygen (typically 2 L by nasal cannula), continuous ECG monitoring; chewed aspirin 160–325 mg and nitroglycerin for pain
claims.quote: A reliable IV route must be established, oxygen given (typically 2 L by nasal cannula), and continuous ECG monitoring started. Prehospital interventions by emergency medical personnel (including ECG, chewed aspirin [160 to 325 mg], and pain management with nitroglycerin) can reduce risk of mortality and complications (1).

claims.text: STEMI: emergency PCI is preferred when it can be done in time (door-to-balloon < 90 minutes, < 120 with hospital-to-hospital transfer) by an experienced operator
claims.quote: For patients with STEMI, emergency PCI is the preferred treatment of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction when available in a timely fashion (door to balloon-inflation time < 90 minutes, or < 120 minutes if hospital-to-hospital transfer is involved) by an experienced operator

claims.text: If PCI will be significantly delayed: fibrinolysis for STEMI patients meeting criteria — goal door-to-needle 30–60 minutes; greatest benefit within 3 hours, may be effective up to 12 hours
claims.quote: If there is likely to be a significant delay in availability of PCI, thrombolysis should be performed for patients with STEMI meeting criteria (see Infarct extent). Reperfusion using fibrinolytics is most effective if given in the first few minutes to hours after onset of myocardial infarction. The earlier a fibrinolytic is begun, the better. The goal is a door-to-needle time of 30 to 60 minutes. Greatest benefit occurs within 3 hours, but the medications may be effective up to 12 hours.

claims.text: Medications for acute MI: aspirin plus prasugrel, ticagrelor or clopidogrel; a heparin or bivalirudin; sometimes a GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor with PCI; usually nitroglycerin for angina; beta blocker; ACE inhibitor or ARB; statin
claims.quote: Antiplatelet agents: Aspirin and prasugrel, ticagrelor, or clopidogrel Anticoagulants: A heparin (unfractionated or low molecular weight heparin) or bivalirudin Sometimes a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor when PCI is performed Antianginal therapy, usually nitroglycerin Beta-blocker Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) Statin and sometimes additional lipid-lowering agents
claims.locator: Pharmacologic treatment of acute myocardial infarction

claims.text: Your EKG notes give V2–V3 thresholds of ≥ 2 mm for men and ≥ 1.5 mm for women.
claims.quote: ≥ 2 mm (men) or ≥ 1.5 mm (women) in V2–V3

claims.text: Merck splits men by age: ≥ 2 mm at 40 or older and ≥ 2.5 mm under 40; 1.5 mm for women of all ages.
claims.quote: or in V2-V3 ≥ 2 mm in males 40 years or older, ≥ 2.5 mm in males younger than 40 years, and 1.5 mm in females of all ages
